 1                                   I.      INTRODUCTION

2    Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, POSITION, AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

3    A.    My name is Alex E. Vaughan. I am employed by the American Electric Power Service

4          Corporation (AEPSC) as Managing Director Pricing, Generation & Fuel Strategy, in

5          the Regulatory Services Department. AEPSC is a subsidiary of American Electric

6          Power Company, Inc. (AEP) that provides corporate support services to the operating

 7         subsidiaries of AEP, including Southwestern Electric Power Company (SWEPCO or

 8         the Company). My business address is 1 Riverside Plaza, Columbus, Ohio 43215.

 9   Q.    PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR RESPONSIBILITIES AS MANAGING

10         DIRECTOR, PRICING GENERATION & FUEL STRATEGY.

11   A.    As Managing Director, Pricing Generation & Fuel Strategy, I assist with the

12         preparation of, and support for, filings before the regulatory commissions exercising

13         jurisdiction over the AEP electric utility operating companies, including SWEPCO.

14         My responsibilities include the oversight of cost-of-service analyses, rate design,

15         special contracts, energy supply costs, and new generation resource approvals for the

16         AEP System operating companies.

17   Q.    PLEASE     DESCRIBE       YOUR      EDUCATIONAL         QUALIFICATIONS         AND

18         BUSINESS EXPERIENCE.

19   A.    I graduated from Bowling Green State University with a Bachelor of Science degree in

20         finance in 2005. Prior to joining AEPSC, I worked for a retail bank and a holding

21         company where I held various underwriting, finance, and accounting positions. In

22         2007, I joined AEPSC as a Settlement Analyst in the RTO Settlements Group. I later

23         became the PJM Settlements Lead Analyst, where I was responsible for reconciling



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                    REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                      1                        ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                   3
  1         AEP’s settlement of its activities in the PJM market with the monthly PJM invoices

 2         and for resolving issues with PJM. In 2010, I transferred to Regulatory Services as a

 3         Regulatory Analyst and was later promoted to the position of Regulatory Consultant.

 4         My responsibilities included supporting regulatory filings across AEP’s eleven state

 5         jurisdictions and at the FERC. I also performed financial analyses related to AEP’s

 6         generation resources and loads, power pools, and PJM. In September 2012, I was

 7         promoted to Manager, Regulatory Pricing and Analysis, where I was responsible for

 8         cost of service, rate design, and special contract analysis for the AEP east operating

 9         companies. In September 2018, I was promoted to Director of Regulated Renewables

10         and Pricing, at which time the oversight of regulated renewable, new generation and

11         fuel filings across the AEP operating companies was added to my responsibilities. In

12         June 2022, I was promoted to Managing Director of Regulated Pricing. I assumed my

13         current position in August 2024.

14   Q.    HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY FILED TESTIMONY BEFORE ANY REGULATORY

15         COMMISSION?

16   A.    Yes. I have presented testimony numerous times before the regulatory bodies in

17         Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia.


18                      II.     PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

19   Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY IN THIS

20         PROCEEDING?

21   A.     My rebuttal testimony responds to various issues raised by Texas Industrial Energy

22         Consumers (TIEC) witness Shawn McGlothlin and Cities Advocating Reasonable




     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                    REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                      2                        ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                    4
  1         Deregulation (CARD) witness Anthony Georgis regarding the Company’s proposed

 2         standard Contract for Electric Service – Large Load (ES-LL Contract).


 3                III.    PROPOSED TARIFF TERMS AND APPLICABILITY

 4   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. MCGLOTHLIN’S RECOMMENDATION THAT

 5         THE COMPANY SHOULD CREATE A NEW ES-LL CLASS?

 6   A.    Not necessarily. The Commission does not need to decide now, without operating

 7         experience, whether a separate class is warranted. That decision can wait until actual

 8         operating data for ES-LL Contract customers becomes available. I would recommend

 9         that the Commission and parties remain flexible on this issue.

10                Mr. McGlothlin is concerned that potential ES-LL Contract customers may

11         ultimately have characteristics that differ from existing Large Lighting and Power

12         Service (LLP) customers, including significantly larger loads and different usage

13         profiles, and therefore may warrant separate class treatment. The Company, however,

14         will not be able to make an evidence-based recommendation on this matter until it has

15         a test year that includes the new large load customers’ billing units, usage profiles,

16         incremental costs and revenues. Because the Company currently has no new large load

17         customers online taking service, any class-determination regarding their appropriate

18         class- treatment would be necessarily speculative. Furthermore, when an ES-LL

19         customer does begin taking service from the Company, it will need to be at existing

20         tariff (LLP) rates. This is because the Company has no other Commission-approved

21         rate schedule for an ES-LL Contract customer to begin taking service until revised rates

22         can be evaluated and approved in a future proceeding, as needed.




     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                      REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                       3                         ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                      5
  1   Q.    IS THE COMPANY OPPOSED TO THE CREATION OF A NEW ES-LL CLASS IN

 2         THE FUTURE?

 3   A.    No. However, the decision to do so should be based on actual test year information

 4         and the resulting class cost of service study to ensure the decision is properly informed.

 5   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. MCGLOTHLIN’S RECOMMENDATIONS

 6         CONCERNING THE APPLICABILITY OF THE NEW ES-LL TERMS? 1

 7   A.    No.       Specifically, I have two areas of concern with his testimony related to

 8         applicability:

 9                1. First, I disagree with his proposal that the MW applicability threshold apply

10                    only to incremental load at the same site or facility.

11                2. Second, I disagree with his proposal that the new ES-LL Contract requirements

12                    apply only to “new types of loads.” 2

13         Company witness Lynn Ferry-Nelson addresses Mr. McGlothlin’s recommendation

14         to increase the applicability threshold from 75 MW to 250 MW.

15   Q.    PLEASE ELABORATE ON YOUR FIRST AREA OF CONCERN.

16   A.    The proposed ES-LL Contract’s applicability should not be narrowly defined to include

17         only new loads at a single site or facility. This is because data center campuses can be

18         built out in a number of buildings across the same or multiple sites, which could be

19         misconstrued under Mr. McGlothlin’s proposed tariff language 3 to exclude such

20         facilities as they are not a single facility but rather a series of facilities. For example,


           1
               Direct Testimony of Shawn McGlothlin at 9-14 (Jul. 1, 2026) (McGlothlin Testimony).
           2
               McGlothlin Testimony at 9.
           3
               Direct Testimony of Anthony M. Georgis at14, (Jul. 1, 2026) (Georgis Testimony).



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                               4                           ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                          6
  1         an operation could have a contract capacity of 300 MW but be broken up into ten 30

 2         MW facilities. Such a configurations places the same amount of incremental load and

 3         system investment needs on the Company’s system as does a single 300 MW facility.

 4         Furthermore, the concept of common control of different new facilities needs to be

 5         recognized to not allow for gaming by new customers. If the tariff applicability

 6         threshold is 75 MW, two 50 MW facilities at different locations owned by the same

 7         parent corporation would have a higher financial exposure to the Company than would

 8         one 75 MW facility. Thus, the proposed ES-LL Contract’s applicability provision

 9         should recognize and apply to multiple smaller facilities with the same ultimate parent

10         corporation that in total meet the minimum MW applicability threshold.

11   Q.    PLEASE DISCUSS YOUR CONCERN WITH THE SECOND ISSUE IDENTIFIED

12         BY MR. MCGLOTHLIN.

13   A.    To be clear, as described by Ms. Ferry-Nelson, SWEPCO is proposing that the ES-LL

14         Contract’s provision not apply to existing customer loads. However, if an existing

15         customer were to expand its operations in the Company’s service territory by 75 MW

16         or more, then the enhanced ES-LL Contract provisions and protections should also

17         apply to that new load because it will impose the same type of incremental cost and

18         risk upon the Company and existing customers as would any other incremental load.




     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                     REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                       5                        ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                     7
  1                            IV.      STRANDED GENERATION COST CONCERNS

 2   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH CARD WITNESS GEORGIS THAT THE NEW ES-LL

 3         INITIAL CONTRACT TERM MUST ALIGN WITH THE DEPRECIABLE LIFE OF

 4         THE NEW GENERATION ASSETS THAT THE COMPANY WILL ADD TO ITS

 5         SYSTEM TO SERVE THE LOAD GROWTH?

 6   A.     No, I do not. However, I do agree that a longer initial contract term for service will

 7         produce a larger resulting financial obligation for the new ES-LL Contract customer.

 8         That, in turn, results in more protections for existing customers. The longest term for

 9         a standard new large load tariff that I am aware of is 20 years.

10   Q.    IS THE RISK OF OVERBUILDING THE COMPANY’S SYSTEM AND

11         CREATING THE POTENTIAL FOR STRANDED ASSETS THAT MR. GEORGIS

12         DISCUSSES 4 OVERLY SIMPLISTIC?

13   A.    Yes, Mr. Georgis’s example does not account for the broader context of system

14         planning and portfolio management. Although the Company is facing the potential of

15         once-in-a-generation system load growth, it must remain focused on long-term,

16         portfolio-based system planning. Just because the Company may have a need to add

17         new supply resources now to meet system needs, it does not mean that the Company

18         will not have multiple opportunities to rebalance the total size and makeup of the

19         generation supply portfolio in the coming years. For example, the Company has

20         roughly 3,400 MW of current generation capacity resources that are potentially set to

21         retire or contractually end by 2040. As these resources retire, or supply contracts end,



           4
               Georgis Testimony at 8-9.



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                       REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                        6                         ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                      8
  1           the Company will have multiple opportunities, and the advantage of multiple years of

 2           operational experience with new large load customers, to rebalance the generation

 3           supply portfolio and adjust the size and terms of new resources. Simply put, it is not as

 4           simple and direct as comparing the approved ES-LL Contract term to the depreciable

 5           life of a new generation asset to determine the reasonableness of the ES-LL Contract

 6           term. Consequently, Mr. Georgis’s concerns in this area are premature and

 7           unreasonably speculative.

 8   Q.      DO YOU HAVE ADDITIONAL COMMENTS REGARDING MR. GEORGIS’S

 9           ILLUSTRATIVE 35-YEAR GENERATION EXAMPLE HE DISCUSSES ON

10           PAGES 6-10 OF HIS TESTIMONY?

11   A       Yes, the illustrative example Mr. Georgis provides is too narrowly focused and does

12           not adequately reflect the reality of system planning and how SWEPCO provides

13           service to its retail customers from a portfolio of supply resources. While the math in

14           his example is correct, the example does not tell the whole story. The main points Mr.

15           Georgis is missing would be the much lower remaining average cost of the new

16           combined cycle plant that the Company’s remaining customers would benefit from,

17           and the time value of money.

18                    To illustrate the flaws in Mr. Georgis’s example, I will use a hypothetical 760

19           MW combined cycle plant, and assume a 17-year initial ES-LL Contract term 5 that

20           coincides with the new plant going into service. As shown below, the average annual

21           cost of service for the new plant would be 45 percent lower for years 18-35 than for



               5
                 Company witness Ferry-Nelson updates the Company’s proposal on the Initial Contract Term in her
     rebuttal testimony and attached Exhibit LFN-1R.



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                               REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                              7                           ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                                   9
  1         years 1-17. This is due to the concept of declining rate base and the 17 years of

 2         depreciation expense Mr. Georgis discusses. This relationship is illustrated in the

 3         following table.

 4                                       Table AEV R-1




 5

 6                Additionally, the revenue requirements for the first 17 years represent over 60%

 7         of the total lifetime revenue requirement for the new plant, and is $1.5 billion greater

 8         than the remaining 18 years of revenue requirements for the hypothetical combined

 9         cycle plant. This is certainly a substantial contribution to system costs to serve new

10         large loads.

11                The timing of replacement resources also matters. If the Company waited until

12         the end of the large load customer’s initial contract term and then, hypothetically,

13         needed to build the same generation facility to serve the remaining customer base due




     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                      REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                       8                         ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                      10
  1         to the standard turnover of a supply resource portfolio, it would cost customers a great

 2         deal more than if they were just continuing to receive service from a now depreciated,

 3         lower-cost asset. For the same hypothetical combined cycle in Table AEV-R1, a

 4         conservative inflation rate of 2.5 percent would yield an installed cost increase of

 5         roughly a billion dollars if one put the same plant into service 17 years in the future.

 6         The difference in the annual revenue requirement for the plant placed into service 17

 7         years in the future is also over $200 million higher on a nominal basis.

 8                Because new large load customers taking service under the ES-LL Contract

 9         would be paying Commission-approved, cost of service-based rates, they would be

10         effectively buying down the cost of new resources for customers in the future even if

11         they only take service from the Company for the length of their initial contract term.

12         Similarly, we would expect that the additional revenue and billing determinants

13         associated with the new large load customers would stabilize rates for non-large load

14         customers during the initial contract term.

15   Q.    ARE THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED ENHANCED TERMS OF SERVICE FOR

16         LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS DESIGNED TO PROTECT AGAINST STRANDED

17         COSTS?

18   A.    Yes, they are. The initial contract term, notice period, exit fee, minimum billing

19         provisions, and collateral requirement work together to protect existing customers from

20         stranded cost risk. The term, notice period, and exit fee define the duration and

21         magnitude of the financial cost responsibility for the new large load customer. The

22         minimum billing provisions establish the minimum level of revenue to be collected

23         from the customer over the contract term, while the collateral provision partially



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                      REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                       9                         ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                      11
  1         secures the minimum financial obligation.       Of course, the Commission has the

 2         discretion to order even more rigorous terms of service (longer initial contract term,

 3         higher minimum bill provisions, more months of collateral, etc.) to the extent it

 4         determines such terms more appropriately balance the interests of the new, large load

 5         customers and existing customers, both of whom SWEPCO is required to serve safely

 6         and reliably.

 7                                         V.    OTHER ISSUES

 8   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. GEORGIS’S RECOMMENDATION THAT THE

 9         APPROVED TARIFF TERMS BE PUBLICLY STATED? 6

10   A.     Yes, I do agree with him on this point. A public, unredacted version of the ES-LL

11         Contract is provided with Ms. Ferry-Nelson’s rebuttal testimony.

12   Q.    WHAT OTHER ISSUES DOES MR. MCGLOTHLIN RAISE IN HIS DIRECT

13         TESTIMONY?

14   A.    He raises two additional issues toward the end of his testimony that I would like to

15         address. 7 First, I agree that the ramp period should be defined clearly as it is in the

16         Company’s affiliates’ approved large load tariffs. As discussed by Company witness

17         Ferry-Nelson in her rebuttal testimony, the Company has clarified that an ES-LL

18         Contract customer may designate a ramp period of no more than five years. Second,

19         Mr. McGlothlin raises the issue of billing based on contractual demands over the ramp

20         period. I agree with him that this issue may be a concern from both a timing and cost

21         causation perspective. For example, a large load customer may have a long ramp


           6
               Georgis Testimony at 6.
           7
               See McGlothlin Testimony at 14.



     SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-07507                                      REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
     PUC DOCKET NO. 58796                         10                      ALEX E. VAUGHAN
                                                                                                      12
 1          period that gradually moves towards a large maximum contract capacity such as 500

2          MW. During that ramp period, the Company is going to be investing in and securing

3          supply resources to meet the customer’s ultimate contract capacity of 500 MW but will

4          only be billing them based on realized or lower ramp period demands. This can cause

5          a timing issue that could result in existing customers contributing more than their fair

6          share toward new system assets that will be utilized to serve the Company’s total

7          system demands, which includes the growth associated with the large load customer or

8          customers. Because of this, it would not be unreasonable to include a new term in the

 9         ES-LL Contract that ensures that non-fuel generation billings during the contractual

10         ramp period are done using the customer’s ultimate, maximum contract capacity rather

11         than the stated ramp period capacity at the earlier steps during the ramp period. This

12         more closely aligns the customers’ billing with the new system costs their growth is

13         causing.

14   Q.    DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

15   A.    Yes, it does.
